items.title: ‘I can’t show my true self too much on LinkedIn’: This 17-year-old AI founder networked his way all the way to the United Nations
items.summary:
Rhythm Bazari, a high school senior in Atlanta, says every networking opportunity he has had came through LinkedIn, including his invitation to speak at United Nations events during high-level week in September. He also says the person who writes on the platform isn’t quite the person he is in real life.

“Every networking thing I’ve done has been through LinkedIn, to be honest,” said Bazari, 17. “I wouldn’t have found out about a lot of stuff if it wasn’t for LinkedIn.” Earlier this month, LinkedIn said the number of members listing “Founder” on their profiles has risen 125% since 2022, with new Gen Z businesses up 275%.

Asked whether there is a LinkedIn Rhythm and a real one, he said, “I think so.” On the platform, he said, “I try to be more service lesson-oriented versus how I am in person.” He added: “I can’t show my true self too much on LinkedIn.”

How he got in 

It started on Instagram. “I see these students who are my age, and I’m like, how are they getting to the United Nations? And I’m not going there,” Bazari said. He began researching and contacted a major UN youth organization, which didn’t respond at first. He then went through a third-party group, the International Organization of Youth, which pointed him to a flagship event near the UN.

People he met there invited him to speak on the “AI and Human Development” panel. “It was very last minute,” he said. “When I got invited, it didn’t feel real, to be honest.”

He spoke at a UN event on AI and human development that had no youth speakers, he said. His pitch: “We’re the generation who’s going to deal with…
items.t: ‘I can’t show my true self too much on LinkedIn’: This 17-year-old AI founder networked his way all the way to the United Nations

items.title: As AI-powered hackers hit Korea’s banks, OCBC’s head of group operations and tech says a cyber breach is a matter of ‘when, not if’
items.summary:
Since September, South Korea’s financial sector has been hit by a rolling wave of cyberattacks , with regulators counting 40 incidents at 37 financial firms, including banks, brokerages, insurers, savings banks and crypto exchanges. Researchers traced the September attacks to Artex, an AI-powered tool that automated the intrusions. 

“With the velocity that cyberattacks are happening, it is a matter of when rather than if,” Praveen Raina, head of group operations and technology at Singapore’s Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. (OCBC), tells Fortune . 

For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster. “I wish I could prevent them—and we’ll try—but what we can control is having the right processes so that we can react quickly to whatever happens,” Raina says.

His strategy consists of two elements: cybersecurity and resilience. “We’re leveraging AI for cybersecurity,” he explains. “With agentic AI attacking organizations, humans cannot keep up with it… it’s the nature of the beast. So, we’re building a defensive AI wrapper around the bank to protect it.”

His team also regularly conducts red-teaming exercises : structured simulations in which a group acts like a real-world attacker to improve their ability to react in the event of a hack. “We practice a lot among ourselves and with other industry players,” Raina says. “We also have a bug bounty program for white hackers to identify [security] issues in exchange for a reward.”

Building in-house 

Raina joined OCBC in 2008 as its SVP in group operations…
items.t: As AI-powered hackers hit Korea’s banks, OCBC’s head of group operations and tech says a cyber breach is a matter of ‘when, not if’

items.title: Mike Cannon-Brookes on the string of accidents that created $35 billion Atlassian: ‘Don’t copy our story … It’s not a model for how to do things’
items.summary:
Today, the enterprise software company Atlassian has a market cap of $35 billion, a revenue run-rate of $8 billion, and 13,000-plus employees worldwide. CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes has a personal net worth of $10 billion, because his ownership of the company was never diluted by VC money when the company was a brand-new startup.

But the funny thing about the origins of Atlassian, back in the early 2000s, is that the company formed largely based on a series of accidents, Cannon-Brookes told Fortune .

“Don’t copy our story. It’s not very good; it’s not. It’s not a model for how to do things,” he said on a lightning visit to Web Summit in Lisbon. 

Cannon-Brookes and cofounder Scott Farquhar took the same course at the University of New South Wales. Both had applied only for courses funded by scholarships. Cannon-Brookes originally wanted to be an architect (and jokes that he still would if he ever got the time). But the finances were not there. “Anyone that was going to give you money to go to university, I applied for all sorts of scholarships,” he said.

Farquhar had also successfully applied for the Australian Defense Force Academy, but his letter of acceptance got lost in the mail. Thinking he had been rejected, he took one of the same scholarships that Cannon-Brookes had: $15,000 (Australian) per year, tax-free, to do a course that was a mix of computer studies and finance.

The course came with a work-experience placement. “We would go to these companies in, like Wisconsin, for six months of installing [Microsoft] Windows” on office desktop computers. This was back in…
items.t: Mike Cannon-Brookes on the string of accidents that created $35 billion Atlassian: ‘Don’t copy our story … It’s not a model for how to do things’

items.title: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds
items.summary:
American consumers helped foot the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs as retailers passed higher import costs on through price increases. Now the refunds are flowing back, and they are showing up in retailers’ profits rather than in shoppers’ bank accounts.

Best Buy and Kohl’s both reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Tuesday, after Target beat expectations last week. Together, the three retailers recognized $387 million in tariff refund benefits in their latest quarters.

The money traces back to February, when the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, invalidating a significant portion of Trump’s tariff regime. As of Nov. 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had certified approximately $128.4 billion in tariff refunds, including interest, and sent them to the Treasury Department for payment, according to a Nov. 10 filing with the U.S. Court of International Trade.

Tariff refunds are boosting retailers’ profits 

Kohl’s reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of just 1.2%, yet its net income jumped to $254 million from $8 million a year earlier. Much of that came from one-time items: a $137 million tax benefit, a $61 million gain from the sale of two properties, and $45 million in tariff refund benefits, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release .

The department store chain has received approximately $190 million in tariff refunds this fiscal year. It now expects those refunds to add $1.03 to its full-year earnings per share,…
items.t: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds

items.title: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits
items.summary:
Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary rehashed a familiar pitch for Americans who want to get rich: spend less, save 15% of every paycheck, and let the gains compound in the stock market.

But when O’Leary faced down 20 Gen Z workers in a Jubilee Media-hosted debate, one participant challenged the traditional bargain between labor and capital. Why should employees spend their lives drawing wages while investors get rich off the surplus value they create?

“Why should all the money we make doing our work, our labor, why should it go to people like you? We did the work,” the participant, a software engineer named Joe, said to O’Leary.

The episode of Jubilee’s YouTube series “Surrounded,” titled “1 Millionaire Boss vs 20 Gen Z Workers,” posted Nov. 15 and put the multimillionaire investor face-to-face with younger workers questioning the rules of the modern economy. The 8-minute exchange over whether workers deserve a bigger piece of the profits they help generate became one of the flashpoints of the nearly two-hour debate.

The argument lands as employee ownership gets a mainstream hearing. SpaceX’s June IPO was expected to make more than 4,400 current and former employees millionaires, welders among them . And Mark Cuban has proposed that companies choose between giving every employee stock and paying higher corporate taxes .

From Starbucks dividends to Amazon stock grants 

Joe opened with a Starbucks hypothetical: Why shouldn’t some of the chain’s billions in profits go to the workers making and serving the coffee? O’Leary argued that would shortchange investors who…
items.t: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits

items.title: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says staff call him a ‘control freak’—but that he learned it from Apple’s Steve Jobs
items.summary:
Airbnb’s billionaire CEO Brian Chesky recently admitted that some of his workers probably call him a “control freak.” But he says he’s in good company, as he picked up the habit from studying Apple’s Steve Jobs. 

“People called him a control freak. He probably was a control freak,” Chesky told Time . “He held people to extremely high standards. He spent a lot of time recruiting. He was in the details.”

When asked whether Airbnb staff would say the same, Chesky responded: “I think some people do.” He also spends 3 hours a day recruiting and tells his hiring managers to leave if they don’t like his input.

But he insists that doesn’t mean he’s micromanaging his workforce—and he even talked to the man who worked closest to Jobs to prove it.

Jony Ive worked with Steve Jobs for nearly 15 years—and said he wasn’t a micromanager 

Apple’s former design chief, Jony Ive, worked alongside the late cofounder for nearly 15 years in designing iconic products like the iMac, iPod, iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. And so Chesky once point-blank asked Ive what it was like working for Jobs.

“Johny said to me, ‘I never felt like Steve was micromanaging,” Chesky recalled, adding that Ive’s felt like they were just “constantly partnering” because Jobs wasn’t outright telling him what to do. He just wanted to be in on the details. They’d even have lunch together every day . “Constantly working back and forth,” Chesky added.

And that’s where the Airbnb boss draws the line. He said “micromanagement, where you’re like telling people what to do” is a last resort—and probably an indicator of how…
items.t: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says staff call him a ‘control freak’—but that he learned it from Apple’s Steve Jobs

items.title: The pig in the python in the marital bed: How boomers deformed the Silent Generation’s marriages, Gen X’s childhood and millennials’ housing
items.summary:
The baby boom has been called “the pig in the python” since at least 1974, when Russell Baker gave the 76 million-strong bulge its name by using the disturbing image of a python swallowing a pig and struggling to digest it, just the way the economy is struggling to digest the bulge of the largest generation in history. It’s becoming increasingly clear, as the baby boomers push the median age of the U.S. population toward 40, that the generation is so big that it has created its own markets as it moves through life.

In the current economy, this market-making dynamic is most visible in housing , where empty-nest boomers own 28% of U.S. homes with three or more bedrooms, compared with 16% for millennial parents, according to a Redfin analysis of Census data. The first-time homebuyer age has jumped to match the record-high median age of 40, the National Association of Realtors found last November.

A new peer-reviewed paper suggests the python bulge was being felt decades ago in the marriage market of the 1970s and the bonanza in divorces that resulted. In an article titled “ The baby boom and the US divorce boom ,” published this month in the European Economic Review , Tereza Ranošová, an economist at the Deutsche Bundesbank Research Center, argues that the two postwar booms, in births after 1945 and in divorces about 25 years later, are linked. The U.S. divorce rate more than doubled between 1960 and 1980.

Ranošová’s explanation is mostly arithmetic. “As men typically match with younger women, a large young cohort presents a supply shock to the remarriage options of…
items.t: The pig in the python in the marital bed: How boomers deformed the Silent Generation’s marriages, Gen X’s childhood and millennials’ housing

items.title: Black and Latino workers are about 20% likelier than White workers to need a new career by 2035 as AI reshapes work, McKinsey says
items.summary:
Black and Latino workers are about 20% more likely than White workers to need to move into an entirely new occupation by 2035 as AI and automation reshape work, according to projections in a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility released Nov. 20.

AI and automation could take over about the same share of work across racial groups, McKinsey projects. What differs is whether that work disappears. McKinsey estimates that automation could reduce an average of 21% of current U.S. work hours by 2035. Of the hours it takes over, 40% of those worked by Black workers and 41% of those worked by Latino workers would be displaced, compared with 37% for White workers and 36% for Asian workers, meaning employers would need fewer people, rather than an augmented environment in which the technology supports a person doing the job.

The report ties the gap to the kinds of jobs people hold. Automation is most likely to replace tasks that are standardized, easy to check and low-stakes when wrong. McKinsey’s example is answering a routine billing question, as opposed to adjusting a patient’s medication dose. Tasks like the billing question make up a larger share of the hours Black and Latino workers put in. Physical work, which is increasingly exposed to robotics, accounts for 35% of Black workers’ hours and 39% of Latino workers’ hours, compared with 26% for White workers.

The jobs most exposed to AI are predominantly held by Black and Latino workers. McKinsey Report 

“Our research indicates that while AI and automation are expected to affect a similar share of work…
items.t: Black and Latino workers are about 20% likelier than White workers to need a new career by 2035 as AI reshapes work, McKinsey says

items.title: Black Friday will put AI shopping agents to the test. Consumers aren’t buying it yet
items.summary:
Earlier this fall Visa instructed 22 different personal AI agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop, and a hair appliance—to see how they’d do. It was not a resounding success. Only 57% of the 15 shopping trips each agent made led to a purchase that matched the shopper’s needs or even resulted in a suggestion of something suitable. 

Many agents misunderstood consumers’ preferences or didn’t know what questions to ask, such as, “Is this TV game-compatible?” leading to many wrong purchases.

The biggest names in retail have spent the year wiring their stores and websites for AI assistants, betting shoppers will soon rely on bots for their buying. Walmart made a big show of supporting agentic commerce early this year when it announced a partnership with Google and its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant to make it easier for shoppers to discover and buy items from the world’s biggest retailer. Target consumers using ChatGPT can now tag the assistant and describe an occasion they are shopping for and get back product ideas they can buy in a single checkout. Home Depot in August expanded its AI-powered shopping assistant, Magic Apron, to all of its stores after an initial limited trial. And earlier this month, OpenAI unveiled its “Wallet” that connects with American Express , Visa and Mastercard to allow agents to pay and close out a transaction based on the limits a human customer sets.

But the Visa simulation illustrates the progress agentic commerce has made and how far it still has to go. This Black Friday-to-Cyber Monday weekend gives AI shopping…
items.t: Black Friday will put AI shopping agents to the test. Consumers aren’t buying it yet

items.title: Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users
items.summary:
Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in users, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.

And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.

In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, said Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she said, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the new era of online information gathering.

In their first year on Reddit, users tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune . The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have users who have over a decade of karma,” Wong said. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in…
items.t: Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users

items.title: I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why | Catherine Fookes

Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills

  • Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

  • Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs


This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills, just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK.

The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains.

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary:
We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.t: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.summary:
Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.
